# Women's Lives

## The principle

> status: ratified (D-0074)

"Bad societies are always bad to women." The health of this society is measured — and
dramatized — by what it does to its women. This must be engaged literally, in the
texture of this particular medieval world: law, labor, marriage, birth, and the
narrow ledgers a woman is permitted to appear in.

## The Austen/Brontë instrument

> status: ratified (D-0073)

The influence that makes this bearable and sharp rather than miserable: women's lives
rendered with perfect plotting, sharp characterization, and strong voice — survival
horror conducted in drawing rooms and on moors. The empire's cruelty to women plays
out substantially in etiquette, inheritance, and arithmetic; the terror is usually
polite ([[influences]]).

## The guardrail

> status: rejected (D-0076)

Explicitly rejected: the Walking Dead / Outlander mode — trauma-drama of awful things
happening and happening to women, suffering as spectacle or shock fuel. Systemic
cruelty is shown as system: cold, economic, mostly off-screen in its worst physical
particulars, never titillating, never the camera's reward. Survivors get interiority,
competence, and dry wit — not just wounds.

## Women's work, criminalized

> status: provisional (D-0074)

Approved directionally: the empire's war on decentralized female economies. The loom
licensed, the home-woven ward outlawed as unstamped goods; midwifery hunted as
untaxable, uncountable care; herb-lore prosecuted as poisoning; the commons of
grandmother-knowledge broken up like any other commons. Not witch-panic superstition —
monopoly enforcement wearing pious clothes ([[information-control]],
[[professions]]).

## The pipeline to sex work

> status: ratified (D-0075)

A society like this has a pipeline from poverty to sex work, and the story
acknowledges it plainly. Widows inheriting dead men's debts, girls priced out of
apprenticeships, the dispossessed of cleared villages — the arithmetic runs one way,
and everyone knows it.

### Session sketches

> status: proposed

Unratified textures: the empire managing rather than banning the trade (licensed
comfort-tents at the labor camps, taxed like any forge); the workers' own informal
guild-craft — shared wards, shared teas, shared knives, a fierce quiet union of
mutual protection; and the story's insistence that these women read as pragmatic
survivors with full interior lives, never props.

## Sexuality and romance in the world

> status: ratified (D-0075)

The world has romance and sexuality — beyond the sexless protagonist and the
post-sexuality anchor. It is part of the flavor of every community the trio passes
through: courtships, marriages good and bad, desire across every class. For the
apprentice, this is bildungsroman material with a hard early edge: before they are
old enough to feel desire themselves, they will encounter people who buy and sell
children — into labor, into marriage — and will learn what their fluid presentation
protects them from. Later, grown, they will feel desire arrive and disturb all their
careful arithmetic. Gender is never the apprentice's chief concern; the plot is.

### The tonal counterweight

> status: proposed

Sketch, unratified: romance as the world's stubborn, inefficient beauty — the thing
the ledger cannot price. Two soot-stained laborers pooling coins for an hour of
privacy; a boy crossing a storm with a bog-flower; a smuggler trading a jar of honey
for a blue glass bead because someone loves the color. The protagonist observes such
things with alien puzzlement while the dead inside her ache with recognition.

## The three tiers

> status: provisional (D-0074)

Approved directionally: women's oppression stratified by class — the keep-aristocrat
(physically safe, socially entombed, her body a merger instrument); the
spoke-laborer (worked, poisoned, her fertility taxed and her widowhood indebted); and
the fringe cunning-woman (free, hunted, and the only one who still owns her
knowledge). The "madwoman in the attic" reclaimed as the woman the system could not
enclose.
